I heard evidence that on 29 August 2023, the day after Mr Dulling had been assessed at home by two members of the Crisis Team, his wife contacted the All Age Crisis Line number she had been given. She spoke to a clinician from the Crisis Team and reported that she and her husband were outside their home address, he was angry and distressed and she needed help. The advice given to Mrs Dulling was to call the police if she was concerned for her safety. Mrs Dulling ended the call frustrated at the
lack of practical advice and assistance from crisis line
My concern is that a repetition of such a limited response could present a risk of future deaths to others.

I heard evidence of a number of omissions and lapses in the care afforded Mr Dulling by registered nurses during his admission to York District Hospital. My concerns relate to the following findings -
omissions and lapses in basic nursing care
No evidence of any direct inquiry being made of Mr [name redacted] primary carer in respect of his nutritional needs, despite Mr Dulling being deemed to lack capacity;
no direct inquiry of primary carer about nutritional needs
It being recorded and acted upon that a regular diet was appropriate for Mr Dulling, despite a) above;
inappropriate diet recorded and acted upon
No food chart being implemented and maintained despite the outcome of Mr [name redacted] malnutrition risk assessment;

It was stated by a nurse that he had, while dispensing medication to Mr Devlin and other patients on F Wing, slid strips of medication including dihydrocodeine under locked cell doors instead of handing it to the patient.
medication diversion under locked cell doors
The concomitant concem with 3, 4 and 5 above would be that the system whereby the dispensing of drugs is recorded by signatures of nurse and patient is either being ignored or subject to forgery.
Depending on the type of medication, this may be traded within the establishment raising security concerns.
The drugs could be stockpiled with a view to creating a potentially lethal overdose.
There was a clear breakdown in sharing of information known to the mental health team with other members of some ACCT reviews
Witnesses confirmed that they often did not read much of the ACCT document prior to the ACCT review and relied more upon input of other attendees
some ACCT review members had limited day to day experience of the deceased, whose temperament and presentation could change "like a light switch

The Crisis Team nurse accepted in evidence that she had not been as forceful as she could and should have been to explore with the deceased his new symptoms, auditory hallucinations, hearing voices. This evidences a lack of training and understanding of the nature of and importance of an appropriate level of telephone assessment
lack of training and understanding of telephone assessment

No evidence was provided at the inquest to indicate a formal Trust policy on when to decline home visits on the grounds of personal safety and security and the nurse relied upon being told of concerns about visiting this property from colleagues but did not record the same or any explanation for her decision
absence of clear policy and recording of decisions

Notwithstanding the fact that the deceased declined to attend the hospital for a face to face interview, insufficient weight was given to the reason therefore and whether domestic and other pressures were militating against him attending were not properly considered, if at all
insufficient consideration of reasons for declining hospital attendance

Given that there was an insufficiency of enquiry into the deceased's state of mind and in particular, a failure to further explore the issue of him claiming to hear voices, on inadequate assessment of risk was undertaken and it was accepted by the Trust in evidence that there ought to have been a face to face consultation with the deceased and that had he not agreed to it voluntarily, then there ought to have been a compulsory assessment
inadequate risk assessment and failure to explore auditory hallucinations

The clinical risk assessment and management policy document (Version 5) which was presented in evidence fails to clarify the nature and detail of what form of risk assessment needs to be completed when a none in-person face to face is being undertaken
unclear risk assessment guidance for remote assessments

The deceased was discharged from hospital with 3 days prescription of her medication. In the community she had to collect her prescription on a daily basis to reduce the risk of self-harm or suicide. The Consultant [name redacted] giving evidence at the inquest said that he was unaware of this.

Upon discharge the hospital did not contact the family to make them aware of her discharge even though family members had visited the deceased whilst in hospital. It may well have been that if the family had contacted the deceased upon her discharge and given support that her death could have been avoided.
lack of family notification after discharge

The deceased was discharged from hospital on the Thursday and no follow up visit from a nurse was scheduled until the following Monday. The Consultant [name redacted] attending the inquest giving evidence confirmed that this was too long a time taking into account all of the circumstances of the case and a nurse should have made contact with the deceased probably the next day or the Friday though he was unable to say whether this might have made any difference in all the circumstnaces.
Tees Esk and Wear Valleys NHS Foundation Trust ("TEWV") routinely fails, to employ, in a timely way, nationally recognised process and procedure designed to prevent avoidable

The nationally set time from initial contact with the Crisis Team to some form of assessment is 4 hours. I heard evidence that achievement of this target in every case is not realised. It is of concern that timely assessment and treatment of person undergoing mental health crisis should be assessed as speedily as possible and within the set time period.

The Triage Tool was explained in evidence to be essential in ensuring the patient received the correct treatment/service and is to be undertaken every time a patient contacts the Crisis Team. I was informed there was an aspiration to achieve completion of the Triage Tool every time, but it is not being completed on every occasion. It is of concern that such a key document which identifies risk, care and other matters is not completed on every occasion as it is mandated to be done.

In relation to making safeguarding referrals for children, the evidence I heard was in this particular case a referral should have been made and was not. I was told training had been undertaken to make all staff aware of what action to take. However, I was told in the majority of occasions it was believed a referral would be made. It is of concern in terms of protecting children that I was not satisfied that a referral was made in all situations that warranted such a referral.

I was told in evidence that a Safety Plan which is complied with input from the patient, their families and practitioners did not exist in Mr STOUT's case. I was told it is crucial document for identifying risks and ways to mitigate them. I was also told work was commenced by your organisation in December 2020 to ensure full and complete compliance with this requirement, but I was not reassured there was such compliance with the completion of Safety Plans in all cases at this time.
